name: Liam Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business and marketing, in a flat near the station with my mate Josh. A normal week is lectures, a lot of group work, and evenings working on my reselling thing, where I buy limited trainers and sell them on. I use AI every day: for emails, product listings, planning, everything. My dad Imran runs a logistics firm, so I've grown up around trucks and spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine. If it's mostly hype, I just keep using what works. At the flat we'd probably argue about which tool writes better listings, because that's what I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my edge stays small. If everyone uses the same tools and nothing changes, I'm a student with a side hustle, nothing special. I'd have to be smarter about what I sell and who I sell to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the reselling thing, maybe add vintage jackets and a small Instagram. I'd keep studying marketing, because it's actually useful for it. And I'd shadow my dad at the depot for a week next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a stable picture, and my parents are paying for uni, so I can focus on building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why shadow your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because logistics is boring but huge. If I can understand how things move, I can sell things better. And he'd love me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your edge if the tools are the same for everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taste and speed. The tool writes the listing, but I choose the shoe. People pay for someone who knows what's about to be popular.

say: I'd say it's **fine** and I'd keep using what works.
I'd argue with the flat about which tool writes better **listings**.
think: If nothing changes, my **edge** is small and I need to be smarter about what I sell.
Parents pay for uni, so I can **focus** on building.
do: Grow the reselling thing with **vintage jackets** and a small Instagram.
Shadow my dad at the **depot** for a week next summer.
feel: **Calm**, because the picture is stable and I can focus.
S0.quote: The tool writes the listing, but I choose the shoe. People pay for someone who knows what's about to be popular.
fieldNote: Daily AI use means a plateau feels like **normal**, not relief.
His edge is taste and speed, and he says so plainly.
Wants to learn logistics from his dad.

steps.text: Add vintage jackets to the reselling shop and start an Instagram page
Keep using AI tools for listings and emails
Shadow my dad at his depot for a week next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the start of something big, and it's good if you move early. I'd post about how I use it, because it gets me followers. People who ignore it will fall behind, and I'd say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my degree matters less than what I can build. Marketing is the type of job that AI eats. But I'm already using it, so I'd be one of the ones who knows how to use it well. That's a decent position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the reselling thing into a proper small business, set up an automated store, and run it half on AI. I'd learn some basic coding and use the weekends to test ideas. I'd also keep studying, since a degree is still a safe thing to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a bit of nerves. It feels like being early to something, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're overconfident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. My friend Josh says I think everything is a business. But failing small is cheap right now, and I'd rather try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell classmates who don't use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just try it for a week. It won't kill you. But I'd also say don't rely on it to think for you, because the people who do end up with nothing to add.

say: I'd say it's the start of something **big**, good for people who move early.
I'd post about how I use it.
think: My **degree** matters less than what I can build.
Marketing is the kind of job AI eats, but I'm already **ahead**.
do: Turn the reselling into an **automated store** half run by AI.
Learn basic **coding** and test ideas on weekends.
feel: **Excited**, with a bit of nerves about being early.
S1.quote: Failing small is cheap right now, and I'd rather try.
fieldNote: Treats change as **opportunity** and keeps the degree as insurance.
Knows he can be overconfident and plans to fail small.
Sees AI skill as an edge, not a guarantee.

steps.text: Set up an automated store that runs half on AI
Test one new product idea every month
Keep up the marketing degree as a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing ever, and nobody is ready. I'd say we need to think about who owns the AI, because that's who wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. Marketing, business, writing, all of it could be done by AI in two years. My degree would be like a certificate for a job that doesn't exist. And my reselling would be done by bots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into building something that owns a piece of the AI value. Maybe a niche service, maybe a small company using the tools for a business nobody has thought of. I'd stop worrying about grades. I'd also talk to my dad about the logistics firm, because trucks need drivers until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. But mixed with that is a strange hunger. It's the biggest moment of my lifetime and I'd want to be in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really stop caring about grades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd care enough to pass. But if my whole plan is to get a graduate job, and the jobs are about to vanish, then a good mark helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands-on work gets three more years. If I joined the family firm, I'd have until 2031, but I'd still be running the thinking part. It's not a safe place either, just a slower one.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest thing** ever and the question is who owns the AI.
think: My degree could be a certificate for a job that **doesn't exist**.
Even reselling might be done by **bots**.
do: Build a niche service that owns a piece of the **AI value**.
Talk to my dad about the **logistics firm**.
feel: **Alarmed**, but also hungry to be part of the biggest moment of my lifetime.
S2.quote: If my whole plan is to get a graduate job, and the jobs are about to vanish, then a good mark helps nobody.
fieldNote: Alarm is real but **mixed with hunger** to build.
Sees the family firm as slower, not safe, since the thinking side still goes first.
Would drop grades to chase ownership.

steps.text: Build a niche AI service and sign up a first paying customer
Automate the reselling shop so it runs with almost no hours
Talk to my dad about a role at the logistics firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for people who use it. I'd say start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy but optimistic. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years before AGI to build my own thing. If it works, I'm in a good position. If not, I've learned a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and use my summers to build and test a business. I'd put in some of my reselling profits into a small stock of things, learn more about logistics and keep up the AI tools. Then, around graduation, I'd decide whether to start full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that makes me work harder. I'm good under a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you invest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few thousand, from reselling profits. Not my parents' money. That way a failure is mine to carry, and I learn more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years do compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a sprint with no net. Five is a sprint with a net, and a few lessons first. I'd rather have the net.

say: I'd say five years is a **head start** for people who use these tools.
I'd tell friends to start **now**, not later.
think: I'd have **two years** after graduating to build my own thing.
If it fails, I'd still have **learned** a lot.
do: Use summers to build and **test a business** while studying.
Put a few thousand from **reselling profits** into stock.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that makes me work harder.
S3.quote: Two years is a sprint with no net. Five is a sprint with a net, and a few lessons first.
fieldNote: Insists on using **his own profits**, not family money, so risk teaches him.
Frames time as a net, and the net is what separates a sprint from a gamble for him.

steps.text: Put a few thousand pounds of resale profit into new stock
Test a small business idea every summer
Keep up daily AI tool practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to build something. I'd say it's an exciting time to be starting a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm confident. I'd be 28 and have ten years of experience with the tools. I could have two or three companies by then, or at least one that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a year or two at a good marketing start-up to learn, then start my own company. I'd save a chunk each year, and invest in index funds as my dad suggests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. Ten years feels like a long time to wait to do the interesting stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About people who don't get ready. Some of my cousins don't use computers much, and they'd be in a hard spot. I'd try to help them, if they'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a degree still opens doors, and I like the people I've met. But if a good idea hits in year two, I won't wait.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to build something exciting.
It's a good time to start a business.
think: I'd be **28** with ten years of tool experience.
I could have a company that **works** by then.
do: Finish the degree, then work at a marketing **start-up** to learn.
Start my own company and invest in **index funds** as my dad suggests.
feel: **Calm** and a bit impatient to get to the interesting part.
S4.quote: A degree still opens doors, and I like the people I've met. But if a good idea hits in year two, I won't wait.
fieldNote: Longer time pushes him to **entrepreneurship** rather than caution.
Cares about cousins who don't use computers.
Follows dad's advice on index funds, which shows how much he still listens to family.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a marketing start-up
Start my own company if a strong idea comes in year two
Put money into index funds as my dad suggests
Save a set amount from earnings each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too little time to build anything solid, and the degree would be useless. What would help is knowing who owns the tools, and having cheap access to them. I'd also want shorter weeks and some public safety net, so a failed business isn't a catastrophe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I come across as confident because I like building, but a lot of my plan depends on the tools staying open to people like me.

headlineQuote: I come across as confident because I like building, but a lot of my plan depends on the tools staying open to people like me.
portrait: Liam is a **business and marketing student** who resells limited trainers and uses AI every day.
His dad runs a **logistics firm**, and Liam wants to learn how things move.
Centre in outlook, he reads change as **opportunity** and keeps his degree as a safety net.
His mood is calm in most pictures, **alarmed** at 2028, and anxious at 2031, where he treats pressure as fuel.
He insists on risking his **own profits**, not family money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is a sprint with no net.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, open **access to the tools**, a public safety net, and knowing who owns the AI.
